title: Series and parallel circuits; Kirchhoff's laws; EMF and internal resistance
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL06-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; EL06-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL06-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; EL06-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL06-1#N.2, EL06-uk1#N.3, EL08-1#N.3, EL06-1#N.4, EL06-uk1#N.5, EL08-1#N.5a, EL06-1#N.7, EL06-uk1#N.8, EL08-1#N.7a, EL06-1#N.10a, EL06-uk1#N.9, EL08-1#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Ammeter
items.clue: Instrument placed in series; an ideal one has zero resistance.

items.label: Open circuit
items.clue: A gap anywhere in a loop, so that no current flows in that loop.

items.label: Short circuit
items.clue: A wire straight across a component, leaving no potential difference across it.

items.label: Voltmeter
items.clue: Instrument placed in parallel across a component; an ideal one has infinite resistance.

questions.stem: Three circuits are each made from an identical cell of negligible internal resistance, a resistor and a lamp. In circuit 1 the three form a single closed loop. Circuit 2 is the same loop with an open switch added. Circuit 3 is the same loop as circuit 1 with a wire of negligible resistance connected directly across the lamp's terminals. Which ranks the currents I₁, I₂ and I₃ in the lamps of circuits 1, 2 and 3?
Three cells are connected in series in a single line: two of emf 1.5 V face one way, and one of emf 2.0 V faces the other way. What is the total emf of the line?
questions.explanation: Right. 1.5 + 1.5 − 2.0 = 1.0 V, in the direction the two 1.5 V cells push.

questions.stem: A battery with an internal resistance of 0.50 Ω drives a current of 0.60 A through a lamp, and an ideal voltmeter across the battery's terminals reads 4.2 V. The lamp is then disconnected, so that only the voltmeter remains connected across the battery. What does the voltmeter now read?
questions.explanation: emf = terminal potential difference + Ir = 4.2 + 0.60 × 0.50 = 4.5 V. With no current, the voltmeter reads the emf.

questions.stem: A 9.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance is connected to three resistors in series. The potential differences across two of them are 2.0 V and 4.5 V. What is the potential difference across the third resistor?
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved round the loop: the three potential differences add up to the supply's 9.0 V. 9.0 − 2.0 − 4.5 = 2.5 V.

questions.stem: A 9.0 V cell and a 3.0 V cell, both of negligible internal resistance, are connected in a single loop with their emfs opposing each other. The total resistance in the loop is 4.0 Ω. What is the current?
A battery of emf 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor. What is the terminal potential difference of the battery?
Resistors of 3.0 Ω, 6.0 Ω and 8.0 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance of the combination?

A 12 V dc supply of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor. What is the current in the 12 Ω resistor?
Cells P and Q have the same emf. P has a smaller internal resistance than Q. Each cell is connected in turn to the same lamp. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The lamp is equally bright with each, as both cells have the same emf.
The terminal pd is larger with P, as less pd is lost inside P.
The terminal pd is larger with Q, as more of the emf is across its resistance.
The current is the same with each, as the lamp alone sets the current.

questions.explanation: Current = emf/(R + r) is larger with P, but lost volts Ir is still smaller, so terminal pd = emf − Ir is larger and the lamp brighter.

questions.stem: A student wants to measure the current in a lamp and the pd across it, but connects the meters the wrong way round. The circuit is: a cell, a voltmeter and the lamp connected in series in a single loop, with an ammeter connected in parallel with the lamp. Both meters are ideal. What does the student observe?

options.text: The lamp is off and both meters read zero, as there is no current in the circuit.
The lamp is off, the ammeter reads zero and the voltmeter reads the emf of the cell.
The ammeter short-circuits the lamp, so a very large current flows through the ammeter.
The lamp lights normally, and the meters show its current and pd as when correctly connected.

questions.stem: A 15 V supply charges a 12 V battery. They are connected in a single loop, positive terminal to positive terminal, and the total resistance in the loop is 2.0 Ω. What is the current, and which way does it pass through the battery?

options.text: 13.5 A, in at the battery's negative terminal and out at its positive terminal
7.5 A, in at the battery's positive terminal and out at its negative terminal
1.5 A, in at the battery's positive terminal and out at its negative terminal
1.5 A, in at the battery's negative terminal and out at its positive terminal

questions.explanation: Right. Net emf = 15 − 12 = 3.0 V, so I = 1.5 A. The larger emf wins and drives current backwards through the battery: that is charging.

questions.stem: A battery of internal resistance r is connected to an external resistor whose resistance equals r. The external resistor is then replaced by one of resistance 2r. How does the potential difference across the terminals of the battery change?

options.text: It stays equal to its first value.
It rises to 2 times its first value.
It falls to 2/3 of its first value.
It increases to 4/3 of its first value.
